title: Australia sanctions two men over Iran-linked antisemitic arson attacks
excerpt: Penny Wong has imposed counter-terrorism financing sanctions on two men the government says organised attacks on a Sydney eatery and Melbourne synagogue.
content_html:
The federal government has placed counter-terrorism financing sanctions on two men it says organised the 2024 arson attacks on a Sydney kosher restaurant and Melbourne's Adass Israel Synagogue on behalf of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong named the two men as Zohair Hassib and Kazem Hamad in an announcement on Friday, 27 November. Neither has been convicted over the attacks. The government alleges they used a complicated chain of intermediaries to carry out the firebombings, according to Reuters.

The listing makes it a criminal offence in Australia to use or deal with the men's assets, or to make assets available to them, the ABC reported. Wong said the measures would limit their access to money and hamper any effort to recruit people for, plan or carry out further attacks.

She described the step as "an important step in disrupting the IRGC's ability to conduct attacks", Reuters reported.

Who the men are

According to the ABC, Hassib holds both Australian and Afghan citizenship and is believed to be in Iran. Hamad, an Iraqi citizen and former Australian resident, was deported to Iraq in 2023, the ABC reported. This is the first time Hassib has been publicly named in connection with the attacks.

The pair join a list of 102 people and organisations that face counter-terrorism financing sanctions in Australia, according to the ABC.

The 2024 attacks

The Lewis Continental Kitchen in Sydney and the Adass Israel Synagogue in Melbourne were both deliberately set alight in 2024. In August 2025, after ASIO concluded the Revolutionary Guard had directed both attacks through a network of proxies, the government expelled Iran's ambassador, Ahmad Sadeghi, and three other diplomats.

Reuters described it as the first expulsion of an ambassador by Australia since World War II. The government also suspended operations at its embassy in Tehran and listed Iran as a state sponsor of terrorism over the Revolutionary Guard's role, SBS reported.

Sanctions enforcement under scrutiny

Friday's announcement came a day after the Australian National Audit Office released a review of the Australian Sanctions Office, the arm of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade that enforces sanctions.

The audit found that none of the 12 matters referred to law enforcement since 2022 had led to a prosecution, the ABC reported. SBS reported that four in five enforcement actions involved warning letters without further follow-up, and that 42 per cent of the 91 investigations completed since 2022 ended with no regulatory action.

The department has agreed to all six of the audit's recommendations. Wong acknowledged the government needed to do more on enforcement, but said the new listings still sent a strong signal to Tehran.
